utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Before we continue to hear the cross-examination of Mr. Mandic, there's a ruling the Chamber wishes to issue orally. The Chamber refers to the accused's sixth motion for filing of disclosure violation and for remedy or measures filed publicly on 9th July 2010, and the Prosecution's response to this motion, filed publicly on 12th July 2010. The Chamber is mindful that one of the remedies sought for the alleged violation of the Prosecution's disclosure obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii) is an extension of the time allocated to the accused for cross-examination of the current witness, Mr. Mandic. The Chamber finds that the Prosecution did breach its Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure obligation by not providing the two documents that are discussed in the motion to the accused at an earlier date. However, having considered the length, which is a total of five pages, and the subject-matter of those two documents, the Trial Chamber is not satisfied that their disclosure by the Prosecution on 7th July 2010 warrants additional time for the cross-examination of Mr. Mandic by the accused. The Trial Chamber will issue a consolidated written decision which will address the remaining issues and submissions -- which will address the remaining -- the remaining issues and submissions raised in the accused's third, fourth, fifth, and sixth motions relating to the alleged disclosure violations by the Prosecution in due course. Well, Mr. Karadzic, let's continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon, Mr. Minister. Good afternoon to all. If I may, just one sentence, please, in relation to the previous question. I believe that this is an invaluable witness, in terms of what he knows, because, in part, he was a participant and, in part, he was a witness. So it would be a pity if he were to leave without us clarifying with him all the things that he can shed more light on, especially in relation to Sarajevo. 1D295, could I have that document now, please. In e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, yesterday we saw that Dobro Planojevic, assistant minister, without any instructions from me, issued instructions of his own, concerning the treatment of prisoners of war and civilians. Let me ask you, Minister, do you remember my anecdotes about general chaos? Remember when I used to say, We have to distinguish between what is ordered by General Mladic and what is ordered by general chaos? Remember that? Do you remember those anecdotes of mine, that we have to make a distinction in terms of who is ordering what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that you asked for your functions to be separated from those of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that I often said that this is a kind of war in which you don't need to give orders saying, Fire, but, rather, Stop?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something seems to be wrong with the document in e-court. Can we have this on the ELMO now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, you confirmed that these instructions of mine were important for the local level, but what about the central organs? We see Planojevic's text. Did they operate regardless of whether I was recommending that or not? Did they operate on the basis of the law, on the basis of the law and international regulations, regardless of whether that had been recommended or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge and as far as I participated in government, all institutions worked on the basis of the law that gave them a certain scope of rights and responsibilities in their respective fields. Mr. Planojevic, as assistant minister for the police, by virtue of his very office, was in charge of issuing instructions from that particular field, as we saw last time, and to issue orders as to how the police should behave in regions and municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's in e-court now, it seems. Could we also have the translation? I believe that there is a translation of this order that you can see here now, so we'll have it in e-court as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You can -- you can get me back. [Interpretation] Yes, this is the Serbian version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Without reading all of it, can you tell us what this document is and when it was issued?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there was a shortage of regulations on imminent threat of war, two months into the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina you issued an order on the observance of International Law of War in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is it that they're supposed to observe; international treaties and what else, 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rules of International Law of War referred to in paragraph 1 of the present item include: International treaties signed, ratified, or acceded to by the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, customary International Law of War, and generally-accepted principles of International Law of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see here that officers are duty-bound to take action and impose sanctions, if necessary. Could you read 3?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this earlier on as well. I tried to explain it when Mr. Tieger was examining me. I said that you ordered the minister of defence, through this order, to issue instructions on the treatment of captured persons. And he specified exactly who was to play which role and how captured persons are to be treated. That includes civilians and prisoners of war who were from the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I asked about this before, and I'd reiterate my request that Dr. Karadzic advise whether a document he's putting on screen is -- was not within the notification of the 1200-plus documents he notified us about. Otherwise, we spend time going through the list unnecessarily. So we would appreciate if we could just be advised accordingly. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you were not informed of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And, again, I'm not suggesting that he should be precluded from using the document, but we should be notified. There may be occasions when the late notice does become relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just waiting for the interpretation. I am sorry, I do apologise, but I believe that that had been the case. This is a very well-known order. It was very important. But we are going to review the matter. We simply do not have enough staff. That is our problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what's the order about? Organising training in the military with regard to these rules, and that finally it enters into force when published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D434.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we're going to see what the minister did in relation to this order. 65 ter 09437, please. It is identical to 1D196. It seems that it's going to be easier to read out the English version. Is this the Official Gazette of the 13th of June, 1992? May I ask for 1D196 in Serbian. It may be more legible. 1D196, could we have that in Serbian? Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, can you tell us, briefly, what is allowed and what is disallowed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of your order, Minister Subotic issued instructions on the treatment of captured persons. Inter alia, he established exactly who is in charge of detaining captured persons, releasing them, what was to be done with these persons, what the powers of the police were, what the powers of the police -- what were the powers of the ministry. He also refers to international regulations and the conditions under which these captured persons can be used for carrying out specific work. Of course, I'm familiar with these instructions. I practically know them by heart.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the rest of the document in Serbian and in English, please. We can have page 2 in Serbian, and in English the participants can see the rest on this page and read out all the items.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is also a reference here to the position of the International Red Cross; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which item?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it's 17.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The representatives of the International Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations shall be enabled to visit and assist captured persons as far as possible."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise once again to the interpreters. I start too early.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are all the rights of detained persons or captured persons. Do you remember a document - if we haven't offered it, we will - where we publicly inform the parents of persons who are captured and kept on our sides, that they should not worry, that they will be tried on the basis of our laws, if they are fit for trial, rather than exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was a proclamation of the Presidency about these captured persons. I think it was given to SRNA News Agency, and it was broadcast on Serb Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Their parents had fled to the federation, and we had no other contacts with them; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the ways in which information could be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this actually a form that was prescribed by Minister Subotic? It was a card that was to be filled out, that this was compulsory documentation accompanying each and every prisoner; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is accompanying documentation, and this is a form that was published in the Official Gazette, along with these instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 09437 has already been admitted as Exhibit P1134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D294, please. Could we just have that briefly. It is a sequel to this form that is to be filled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, while we're waiting for that, let me ask you whether some of those judges who had been appointed left eventually for different reasons; tensions, general anxiety, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there were cases when persons both of Serb and non-Serb ethnicity left. They either took different offices or they left the war-ravaged Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, there was a great deal of fluctuation of personnel. People were coming and going.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we disregard that previous number, because it's part of a document that was already adopted. 65 ter 176, please, can we have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that only depend on them, Minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on them, their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please cast a glance at this document. Could you briefly tell us what this is and when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are minutes from the 28th session, from the 15th of June, 1992, and it was chaired by the deputy prime minister, Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a government session; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, yes. It is one of the government sessions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 4 in Serbian, and perhaps it's the last page in English. Sorry, the fourth one in the document, but it's actually page 5 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, Minister, that at this point in time the government is waging a battle for the functioning of government, as such? Can you look at paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The session indicated how exceptionally important it is for authority to function in all parts of the republic, as well as life itself; inter alia, republican commissioners are supposed to help that process, and they are representatives of all organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing all of that in mind, the government points out the need to have a joint meeting of republican state bodies with the purpose of discussing open or outstanding issues, the synchronisation of activities and measures, and ensuring that work and tasks are conducted in a co-ordinated and efficient manner and within the Constitution and law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read out the last paragraph, please, the one after that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was pointed out was the necessity to find possibilities for distributing the post and other material in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you finish?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To that end, the possibility of providing a helicopter or ultimately a messenger service as a last resort should be considered."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Minister. Does that mean that electronic links could not really meet the needs of the government for a two-way communication with the local level? So what does this mean at the end of the Twentieth Century; courier, Pony Express, what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, that means that the seat of government and republican organs were terribly isolated. The road network barely functioned, and with a large -- and we did not have any communication with a large part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be admitted, if it hasn't been admitted already, that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that has already been admitted as Exhibit P1095.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 65 ter 177. These are all minutes from the sessions of different bodies, and there is an agreement, in principle, that they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a government session. It was -- it is the 29th session, held on the 16th of July [as interpreted], 1992, which was chaired by Professor Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see Serbian page number 4, bearing the number "379," and the corresponding English page, "Re-8" and "9."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please either tell us what the first two sentences of Article 9 are or read them out for us.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The government was informed about the content of the letters sent by the SAO Birac."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version has to be -- well, yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It was assessed that a political and security situation in this region was not satisfactory and that all measures needed to be undertaken to step up security to a higher level."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Minister, please tell the participants, what is Birac? Does it contain Sekovici, Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Milici, Bratunac, and Zvornik, all these municipalities? Is this this group of six municipalities in Eastern Bosnia, the majority of which was accepted to be part of the Muslim territorial unit at various conferences held on the subject-matter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we sent them a proclamation that they should not fight because perhaps their regions would fall to their territorial unit anyway, and it was -- it didn't make any sense for them to fight for it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If we have not offered this already, we shall do so on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that despite all this, they severed our communication, namely, the road Vlasenica to Zvornik, via Konjevic Polje, so that we had to go there via Ceparde?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in several instances at Ceparde, too, was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was my next question. Do you remember that they laid ambushes in -- at Ceparde and at Crni Vrh and that they killed people in civilian vehicles; in fact, a bus was riddled with bullets and many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that at Crni Vrh some people from Rogatica got killed. Some drivers from the Birac mine were also killed. And mainly civilians who were on their way towards the River Drina and on towards Bijeljina or to the right, towards Zvornik, also came to harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that we took military actions in that zone only in -- late in autumn 1992 and in the spring of 1993, when they started attacking the army, also when they started shooting in the backs of troops, and they actually sought shelter in these villages?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at AD-11, the second paragraph. It is the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move on, just for clarification: You read out the item number 9, which refers to SAO Birac, and you were asked about some questions relating to -- some six municipalities in Eastern Bosnia. Were we talking about the same region? The "Birac" refers to those Eastern Bosnia regions? Because I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Birac is a region, Your Honours, which is in Eastern Bosnia, and it encompasses these six municipalities, Zvornik, Vlasenica, Milici, and the other two or three that were enumerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to inform us about this second paragraph of item 11.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was noted that the government should be more active in exercising its constitutional and legal rights and obligations. It was also said that there were certain difficulties posed to the work of the government by the inadequate and insufficient co-operation with the Presidency of the Republic and the Main Staff of the army, and some difficulties and problems in establishing contacts with the regions and the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another piece of proof that there was no good communication.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be only repeating myself if I said that the government as well as the other organs were totally isolated at Pale and on Mount Jahorina and that all sorts of communications were poor and very inadequate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page, 381, please. I believe that in the English version, it is also the last page. Well, then it is the penultimate page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is mid-July -- mid-June. Do you agree that these difficulties with communications lasted for as long as you were a member of the government, at least? Did anything improve?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is mid-July, and we had to grapple with these problems throughout the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall be revisiting this -- the crisis in the Birac region in another document, but now let us see what the last three paragraphs are, what it was that the government dealt with at this session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was concluded that a helicopter should be requested from the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic to be used by the government to establish contacts with the municipalities. The government was informed of the letter of the minister of health, in which all state and international institutions are requested to lift the blockade in order for the necessary medicaments for the Bosnian Krajina to be secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this refer also to the prohibition of delivering oxygen because of which 12 prematurely-born babies -- because of the lack of which, 12 prematurely-born babies died, because they didn't have the necessary oxygen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eleven babies died, and the twelfth baby remained handicapped for life because she didn't receive the assistance she required, actually, the treatment -- the oxygen she needed. Now she's 18 years old. She just turned 18, Mr. President, a couple of months ago, but she's physically disabled and mentally disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am afraid that she, too, has died. Her name is Sladjana, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. No, there was a programme about her on the occasion of the 18th anniversary of that event, and that baby is still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that that drama was the reason for the establishing of a corridor in Posavina and the liberation of that part so as to be able to supply Bosnian Krajina, i.e., the Banja Luka Krajina, with the necessary supplies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were multiple reasons for that, but through arms struggle, a corridor was breached through Posavina, and then the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina could be reached as well as the parts across the Sava River towards Biha [as interpreted] from where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this last one, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government concluded that all measures should be taken, including military measures, to lift the blockade on the Bosnian Krajina and ensure regular supplies of food and other merchandise -- other goods.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for explaining this. Can this be admitted, if it has not been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D199, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, for future purposes, the Judges are not well-aware of the geography in the region, so if you talk about the corridors of some regions, it may be a good idea to show the maps from time to time. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your suggestion. I hope that with this witness we shall identify both the positions around Sarajevo and the settlements around Sarajevo, as well as the principal regions, Birac and the others ones that we have been mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, is this the 20th of June, the political/security situation information of the 2nd Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page in Serbian, and in English that is all that has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what this is about, in a nutshell, in the two highlighted framed parts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Of late, we are encountering the ever-more marked practices of robbery and war profiteering among individuals and groups. Our unit commands, security organs, military police, and organs of social structures have been ordered to discover and prevent such criminal actions. To that effect, a number of groups and individuals have been arrested, and legal action has been taken against them, but we should like to stress that this will be very difficult to eradicate without your help and specific evidence."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was "eradicate;" right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "eradicate." "It is hard to eradicate without," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We would like to draw the attention of also unit commands and officers that pending the adoption of the Law on the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and subsidiary legislation, they should fully abide by the Law on Total People's Defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in particular when pronouncing educational and correctional measures, and rules which regulate the types of educational and correctional measures, and the jurisdiction for their pronouncement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that at that time we still did not have a law on the army and that both the army and the civilian leadership, under such circumstances, actually followed -- abided by the previous laws of the previous federal state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be adopted, admitted? And if the OTP has the entire translation, we would not object to it's being admitted. Can we see the entire Serbian version so that we can see that it is written on it "Confidential"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the first page in B/C/S. Mr. Mandic, what is this document about? Is it an order or a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report on the political and security situation in the Krajina region, which was under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Addressed to who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Addressed to the Presidency, i.e., to the republican institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking because it's difficult to understand how a assistant commander for something in the corps can address the Presidency directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He couldn't do so without approval from his commander. If he had been so empowered or so authorised by him, he could do so. You are right, Your Honours. Without the approval, without the consent of the corps commander, he could not directly address the republican institutions of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see a passage in this document that it was addressed to the Presidency, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, but letters of this kind were mainly addressed to the Presidency, as the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The documents of this kind go upwards to the top, towards the organs, and also downwards, towards the lower-ranking commands?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports, memos of this kind, would be submitted to the competent higher-ranking commands, and the instructions and orders for the execution of instructions contained in them would be submitted to the lower-ranking commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that this was intended to the commands, to the assistant commander for moral guidance, I believe, which was according to his line of work? We happened to stumble upon this example in the archives. So this was sent to the assistant commander for moral guidance and the officers in charge of the same subject-matter at lower levels?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular copy was for the archives, for the file and the assistant for moral guidance, but obviously it was addressed -- the document was addressed to superior commands to inform them about a political security situation in the region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It does -- nevertheless, seems to me -- what does this mean, "PKZ," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander for moral guidance and education.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that we have only partial translation, we'll mark it for identification, pending full translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D436, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have 65 ter 121. I don't know whether it's been admitted. This is a session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's 65 ter 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At this session, the reconstruction or reshuffle of the government is mentioned for the first time, under B. So let's look at item B.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: AD-3, item B: "It was concluded that the prime minister proposed the reshuffling of the government as well as appropriate regulations related to the reshuffle."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the prime minister here was given what belongs to him, the freedom for a cabinet reshuffle?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that as early as late May or early June there were misunderstandings between the prime minister and the premier and that it was recommended to him that instead of replacing people he should conduct a reshuffle?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. So the Presidency told him that he could go ahead and have a government reshuffle; was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 65 ter 124. 124, that's the 14th Presidency Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to present to us items 1 and 2 so that we can see the way in which attempts were made in July to establish the state organs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Presidency adopted the following decisions and conclusions: "1. The decision that the seat of the Supreme Military Court and Prosecutors' Office should be in Han Pijesak."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need a translation also. This is 65 ter. I believe there must be an English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Government of the Serbian Republic, the Ministry of Defence, is ordered to draw up a text of the decision in connection with the appointment of judges and prosecutors. It was agreed that the authorities on the ground should be asked for their opinion of individual candidates so that the best judges and prosecutors can be selected."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where are you reading from? What I see on my screen is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1 on page 1 of the minutes of the Presidency session of the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now we have the Serbian version. We're just waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do have English translation on our own PCs, so if you wish, you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't. We're obviously not using the same system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So opinions are sought on the ground about the candidates?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The seat of the Supreme Military Court and Prosecutors' Office is established in Han Pijesak, and candidates are sought on the ground, and opinions about the candidates also sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where was the seat of the civilian Supreme Court? Now we can see what it was like for us at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are now fixing it, so just bear with us a minute. It should be with you very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us where the seat of the civilian judiciary was; that is, the Supreme Court and the main republican prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, their seat was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a weekend cottage, is that right, next to Hotel Panorama?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An annex of Hotel Panorama.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about items 2 and 7, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2: "The Presidency issued an order to the MUP of the Serbian Republic to conduct an investigation into the activities of paramilitary units on the territory of Gacko and Nevesinje municipalities. "It was said at the session that the Presidency was receiving unreliable reports that groups on that territory, which were not under the command of the army or the police, were terrorising and taking vengeance on the civilian population. The MUP was, therefore, given the task of investigating and preventing the activities of these independent groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have item 7, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 7: "It was concluded that responsible organs shall urgently take the harshest measures against perpetrators of criminal offences and persons spreading disinformation and panic among the population."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page, the next page, that is, so that we can see the end of the document and the signature; in English, too, the last page. Thank you. May this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we go back to item 7 and item 2. Mr. Mandic, do you remember any results of such investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It was the Ministry of the Interior, it was the police, that conducted these investigations, as did the military police. I was in the Ministry of Justice, so I'm not familiar with the results of their investigations. Possible results of their investigation would have been dealt with in the military courts because these were armed paramilitary groups so they would fall under the competence of the military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although they are not members of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although they were not members of the army, armed persons in wartime fell within the competence of the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D438, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have 1D203 and glance briefly at this order which was issued on the same day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the order referred to in the previous document, in item 2, Mr. Minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely what I explained to Their Honours. We can see from this that the investigation was carried out by the police of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these are the paramilitary units we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll soon come to a document where we inform the public they should not be upset, because the persons we arrested were not patriots and they were not regular soldiers, but, rather, they were criminals. We might have a translation. Maybe that's why Mr. Tieger is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document currently on the screen, 05897.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me read in English briefly. Thank you. It will be admitted, unless it has been already admitted. It will be Exhibit D439, then?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it hasn't been admitted, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit D439.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 65 ter 125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. One further question. I'm asking too -- intervening too much, but, Mr. Mandic, as you said, the paramilitaries fall under the purview of military court; then the order to the MUP to investigate what paramilitary did is a wrong order. Am I correct? Mr. Karadzic should have ordered the Ministry of Defence to investigate such acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Ministry of Defence is a civilian organ of state administration, and it cannot carry out investigations directly. Along with the MUP, Mr. Karadzic might have issued an order to the Command of the Herzegovina Corps and the military police of that corps to investigate what was happening on their territory. Probably, in July, Mr. Karadzic had more confidence in the police because the police were able to investigate any crimes occurring on the territory of the entire republic. And when the police concluded its investigation, before criminal proceedings are instituted, they would hand over their results to the prosecutors' office that was in charge of that, so they would have to investigate the groups that came to wage war in Bosnia and Herzegovina which were looting the people and doing everything mentioned in the minutes of the Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, do you agree that the Herzegovina Corps was quite small and few in numbers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it covered Eastern Herzegovina. And it's correct, it was a very small corps, as far as manpower goes, and the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the military police were often at the front-line instead of engaging in police work and that this might have been the reason why we addressed this to the military -- to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had at constitutional right, Mr. President, to involve the police in any form of crime prevention, regardless of whether they fell under the purview of the civilian or the military courts. On completing their investigation, the police would hand over the case to the relevant prosecutors' office, whether civilian or military. So you did not make a mistake when you involved the civilian rather than the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there was some rivalry between the police and the army, as there is everywhere?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the provisions of the Constitution, when there is an imminent threat of war the civilian police was subordinated to the military command, especially in areas where there was armed combat. And, in a manner of speaking, it was the army that was in command of the police in certain situations, as far as combat goes, and the army could order the police to engage in combat. Of course, as is the case with all structures, there was some rivalry, as you say, and occasionally there were conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you believe either one of these structures if, in their reports, they besmirched one another? Would you believe them or would you think that this was a result of their rivalry and misunderstandings?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only give you my opinion. I wouldn't believe anyone. Of course, I would investigate and establish who was right and who was wrong, and punish whoever was to blame. But, of course, the military command felt superior in a situation of an imminent threat of war. And in certain situations the army disobeyed even you, although you were their commander-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at these minutes from the 15th Session, three days later, and let's see what was proposed in item 4, a division of labour in the Presidency. Could I now ask you to read out the first paragraph, AD-1.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In connection with the first item of the agenda, Dr. Nikola Koljevic stated why he was discontent with the work of the Presidency. He stressed that he was discontent with his own performance. He could not endure the work physically or psychologically. He stressed that he was having family problems which affected his contribution to the work of the Presidency. He observed that the efficiency of the Presidency was low."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. We can stop there. Do you agree that the Presidency would work late into the night and that the effects, as the late Professor Koljevic noted, were very small and did not satisfy us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not familiar with the system of the work of the Presidency, and I really cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at number 4. Can you tell us what the problem there was, this regional arbitrariness, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: AD-1.4. So, point 4: "The option was suggested that he go to Krajina to crush Krajina separatism. However, he believes that it would be counterproductive because they could become too attached to him, which might cause more damage."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The previous paragraph says that he, as a person from Banja Luka and Krajina, should go to Banja Luka and curb this behaviour of extreme autonomy in Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that was actually a lack of co-ordination and control, and this affinity of the Serbs to behave in such a way, and that that led to what happened in the weeks that followed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think, Mr. President, that the SAOs were a mistake in the organisation of the state -- or, rather, Republika Srpska, because, in that way, mini-states were created in which all branches of government existed; the executive, the judiciary, the legislative. And, of course, right-wingers that we heard about here at this trial made inappropriate decisions and had inappropriate views at that given point in time, especially at the beginning of the war. It seems to me -- well, it is my opinion that, in a way, this worked to our detriment and it back-fired. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Plavsic pointed out that it would be counterproductive if anyone resigned from his or her position in these times because it would lead to harmful political consequences, and Dr. Koljevic withdraw and his family put up in Belgrade, and what was it that Djeric said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Professor Branko Djeric said that the results of the work were still significant, despite Dr. Nikola Koljevic's self-criticism."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "As he said, improvisational work cannot continue. The Presidency operates without a division of tasks. Closer co-operation with government departments is necessary. He proposed that working bodies of the Presidency be established. He did not agree with the statement that little had been done in the Presidency."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that after that, we carried out this division, and Mrs. Plavsic was put in charge of humanitarian work and co-operation with UNPROFOR in that sense, and foreign affairs were handled by Koljevic and Buha, and I was in charge of military affairs and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Professor Plavsic was in charge of humanitarian organisations and exercising control over the prisons and detention centres at local level where non-Serbs were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read out what I said, what Radovan Karadzic said? It's the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dr. Radovan Karadzic pointed out that we can not be dissatisfied with our performance. It was important that we existed, even if we did nothing, because the Presidency was a symbol of the statehood of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Office of the Presidency, the collective Presidency at that point in time, was it not to represent the country and to co-ordinate work among the legislative and the executive?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like the Queen of England.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Having tea with guests?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on, it says that Professor Koljevic said that he was not dissatisfied with the work of the Presidency, but with his own contribution. He pointed out that he could not control the republican commissioners and considered that to be his own failure. And further down it says that Professor Djeric said that the government and the Presidency did not have proper accommodation, and so on. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you remember, Mr. President, we, as the government, were staying at that hotel on the top of Mount Jahorina. We did not have any proper facilities. Several times, we tried to move the government to the municipality of Ilidza where there were telecommunication links, after all, and all other links. However, that did not happen. So we really worked in very difficult and complex conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, do you agree that commissioners were introduced in order to establish some kind of link between the central organs and the municipalities, and that that was proposed by the leader of the opposition party, Dr. Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in some way to exercise control over the municipal organs on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we see that after, what, a month or so, Professor Koljevic feels helpless and feels that even that did not ensure proper communication between the central organs and the periphery, or, rather, the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is this a government session on the 8th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have page 4 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see the agenda here. We actually saw it. And I see that this part was translated. Item 9 on the agenda, in Serbian, could you read the fourth paragraph: "On the basis of experience ..." et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the basis of experience acquired in SAO Semberija and Majevica, it has been concluded that the decision on the establishment of war commissioners in municipalities, in a situation of imminent threat of war or when at war, cause a certain confusion that needs to be clarified as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read the next one.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It has been concluded that material be prepared on this. The problems, difficulties, obscurities, and the like should be pointed out, and measures should be proposed. After that, the government would, if necessary, submit an appropriate proposal to the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the next one; could you read that as well, "... at the session ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "What was particularly pointed out at the session was that it was indispensable for the government and the ministers to exercise their rights and responsibilities based on law incessantly in the field. Therefore, it was concluded that visits to the SAO of Bosanska Krajina should be planned as soon as possible, but to other regions as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And further on it says that there should be a proposal of a decree how the ministries should function outside the seat of government, and also that the SAOs should be abolished and that the Constitution should be amended; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the SAO were a constitutional category, then the Constitution had to be amended and these autonomous provinces had to be thrown out of the Constitution. That is why the Constitution was being amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, 11, and 13. Actually, it is paragraphs 11 and 13. It's probably the next page in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 1: "The government has been informed about the level of organisation and work of judiciary organs in certain regions prepared by your ministry, the Ministry of Justice." And can you read this page further on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It has been concluded that great problems exist because judiciary military organs have not started to work yet. "That is one of the greatest obstacles in establishing law and order, legality, and a state based on the rule of law in present conditions. "Bearing this in mind, it has been concluded that a proposal be made to the competent authorities to form and qualify as soon as possible a public prosecutors' office and courts, as soon as possible. "It has also been concluded that, due to emergency, the possibility of delegating authority from military to regular judiciary organs be examined and, if necessary, amendments to appropriate laws should be proposed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In mid-July, is the situation such that we do not have a military judiciary yet and that there is a feeling of powerlessness on the part of the state to regulate crimes in that area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is an imminent threat of war, a vast majority, over 95 per cent of crimes committed, all types, all levels, fall under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page. Just one sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Therefore, all regulations have to be passed. Organs, organisations, and institutions have to be established which would actually ensure the existence of a state."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, unless it hasn't been admitted already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we take a break, just one question, Mr. Mandic. Can you go back to the previous page, item 11 and 13.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 11 and 13 in Serbian as well, please. The next one in Serbian. Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. There, it has been concluded, it notes, that it be proposed to the authorised organs to form and qualify the Public Prosecutor' Office and the courts for work as soon as possible, and also that, for emergency reasons, the possibility of authority delegation from military to regular judiciary organs be examined and that, if necessary, amendments to the appropriate laws be proposed. Do you remember what happened afterwards, pursuant to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Justice, as Mr. Tieger knows, I think, as well as Ms. Korner, wrote about this twice in order to have this conclusion carried out. Unfortunately, the Constitution deals with the military and civilian judiciary, so the Constitution had to be amended. During August and September, I think, I asked for this to be carried out, because we had organised the civilian judiciary and prosecutors' office better than the military did, and most of the problems were in the field and fell under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary. So, Your Honours, the proposal I made was that within the civilian judiciary, military departments be established and civilian departments as well, with appropriate jurisdiction, in order to use the judges and prosecutors who were already there and who could deal with these crimes committed both in the military and in the civilian area. The civilian organs were more professional and better organised. Until the government fell, that is to say, until that session that was held in Zvornik on the 23rd of November, that did not happen because the military was opposed to this. They thought that the civilian judiciary was taking over their powers that had been there for many, many years in the former Yugoslavia. That was not true. The intention of the civilian Ministry of Justice, or, rather, the government, was to start working and to start prosecuting individuals or, rather, paramilitaries, all of those who were violating criminal law to a large extent. You will see two of my written communications, and you can also see the stenographic notes from the Assembly where General Gvero and I were -- we simply clashed. He was the person who was in charge of that segment in the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to see those communications, but I wonder in what method we can see the document. Mr. Tieger can help us later on. Could you identify --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have just prepared that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for 25 minutes. We'll resume five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Mr. Karadzic: Have you prepared the documents which you alluded to present to the witness to get brief confirmation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has given the Prosecution most of these documents, which are mainly news reports, but I believe that some of the documents from the government and by the minister, himself, we will be giving to the minister to look at them in his spare time and to initial those which he's familiar with and which he confirms. But that notwithstanding, Excellencies, I believe that it would be a pity, and I'm sure the minister will be angry at me now - it won't it's first time, however - that it would be good if he remain here on Friday as well, because we will not have a witness of this kind for some time to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber's anticipation is that he may be able to conclude his evidence by tomorrow, so you may ask that during the course of today's evidence, to the witness. Let's move on. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I thought the Court was going to -- if there's no issue about presenting documents to the witness, then I -- other than in court, then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Admission is a separate matter. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see 1D204. This is a document from the year 2000. I believe that we do not have a translation, but this is your document, Mr. Minister, from the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you identify it, first and foremost, and then tell us what the second paragraph is about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a letter from the Ministry of Justice, addressed to the president of the Presidency. And, yes, I can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 10th of July, 1992. In fact, this is my very first letter to you, where I propose how the judiciary should be organised; that I already talked about in describing the situation to Their Honours before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that in the first paragraph you inform me and the Presidency that you had carried out the organising and the establishment of regular courts of public prosecutorial offices, as well as municipal misdemeanor courts in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, except in Northern Bosnia, the Doboj region, where it was not possible to do because of the war actions, and that you were also -- that that was also in course? Can you please read paragraph 2, for it to be interpreted slowly, because we do not have a written translation. Am I right when I say that you are sending this to the Presidency, because the Assembly is not convening regularly yet?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first and the second paragraphs or just the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have re-told the first paragraph, and if you can read the second one. I meant the Assembly was not convening and that is why you were sending this letter to the Presidency. And if the Assembly -- had the Assembly convened, you would have sent it to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how I understood it: "By monitoring the situation in the area of the commission of crimes, a large number of committed crimes has been observed from the jurisdiction 'ratione materie' of military judicial organs which still have not been established. Therefore, we propose that regular judicial organs, pending the establishment of military judicial organs, take over their duties on a temporary basis. Thereby, we would considerably contribute to the prevention of the commission of these crimes and contribute to the establishment of a legal order and legal security throughout the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, the ministry states its opinion that there should be amendments to the Law on the Execution of Criminal and Misdemeanor Sanctions, et cetera. And read the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Namely, persons sentenced to a term of imprisonment of up to five years would be sent to serve their sentences only after the end of the war, while in the meantime they would be engaged in military units. Persons sentence to a term of imprisonment of over five years would be sent to serve their sentences upon the finality of the respective judgement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In this connection, it would be prescribed that prescription period for the execution of these sanctions would not include the time while the convict is in the military unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this, Mr. Minister: So you proposed -- the ministry proposed that persons who were to serve sentences up to five years would serve their sentences after the end of the war. Did it ever happen that we released criminals in order for them to join some units, and, to the best of your knowledge, was this also done -- was this done by the other side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I know for a fact that persons who had been sentenced to terms of imprisonment were not released in order to be engaged in the army. As for the other side, I know, at least as far as Sarajevo is concerned, that there were some big-time criminals who were the leaders of some units of Bosnia and Herzegovina's army. They were convicts. Now, whether that was a widespread practice, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page to see the signature and the stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature and stamp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, Excellency? This is one of those documents of a series that you inquired about in connection with what the minister was proposing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D199, please, or 65 ter 11480. 65 ter 11480.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been admitted as Exhibit P1136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, as soon as we get the English version, would you please read the entire letter. It's not too long.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is addressed to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Dr. Radovan Karadzic: "The Ministry of Justice has sent to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina a letter number 01-119/92 of the 10th of July, 1992, in which it is proposing that regular courts and public prosecutors' offices should temporarily, pending the establishment of military judicial organs, take over the jurisdiction of military courts and military prosecutors' offices. The Presidency has not informed this ministry about its position on this proposal. That is why we are hereby again submitting this letter to you with the request that you inform us about further activities and measures." This was signed by my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it relates to the letter that we just saw a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In fact, this is a reminder, a reminder -- a follow-up to that previous letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You expected the Presidency to agree -- to reach agreement with the army, within the space of three weeks, that they actually renounce their powers in this field for this idea to be put into practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P1105, which is minutes from the session held on the 23rd and 24th of November in connection with a reshuffle in the Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that session, I spoke -- I spoke at an Assembly session, in fact, and I proposed that the powers of the military judiciary should be temporarily delegated to the civilian judiciary. And Milan Gvero, who was in charge of the military jurisdiction, discussed this with me. As this is a constitutional category, the president of the Assembly, the speaker, proposed that the item on the agenda be postponed, pending possible amendments to the Constitution, whereafter we would proceed to a reshuffle to change the respective jurisdictions of the military and civilian judiciaries. As at that session, the prime minister, Mr. Djeric, resigned, and I went to Belgrade. I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Serbian page 88 and English page 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And tell us succinctly what it was that you advocated at this session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Serbian 88, English 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last sentence in the Serbian version: "We have another item, a proposal of a decision for combining military and civilian prosecutorial offices and the judiciary."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a proposal sent to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in Serbian, and in English also. Sorry, it is the previous page in English and the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your contribution -- this is your speech, Mr. Mandic. Without reading it, please just tell us the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have stated, I have already partly explained to this Honourable Court that I asked that the civilian and military judiciaries be combined, put together, because the military judiciary was not operational, it was not efficient; and, in contrast to it, the civilian judiciary was mainly well-established, but there was no work because of the situation, because of the state of an imminent threat of war. Mainly, the professional judges from the former system, as well as prosecutors, were sitting in the civilian judicial system, but they were not working. There was a huge accumulation of problems in the field. The gravest crimes against life and limb and against property were being committed. There was violations of international conventions of human rights and freedoms from 1949, as well as other documents. And in seeking a way of how to render operational the rule of law, put into practice the rule of law, the ministry also consulted some professors, for instance, Professor Kokolj from the Faculty of Law in Mostar, and proposed that we combine -- put together the two judicial systems in order to put into practice and establish the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just explain something. You say you know -- you say that whenever we are at Assembly sessions, we criticise both systems, they are not operational, the number of perpetrators and of crimes is growing; and you say we have to solve this, and we have to process Serbs -- prosecute Serbs. Then you go on to say that there are so many judicial -- holders of judicial offices whom we have elected, but we do not have a complete system, neither the civilian nor the military judiciary, but crime is growing. And towards the end, you say: "Judges have come to see me, complaining of the way on-site investigations were carried out. A military police and a military investigation officer go to the site, and there are big problems," and so on and so forth. Is this the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my very words which are recorded here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I recommend to the participants to read this for themselves. Can we go -- scroll down to see what Mr. Krajisnik says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters also have it on the screen before Mr. Karadzic proceeds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Let us hear the military, too, and let the initiative be addressed to our constitutional commission, and let us put in charge our ministry and our Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we see the next Serbian page, and the English, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "They are to co-ordinate that material, that it should be dealt with at the session." That is my proposal. And then General Gvero responds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I therefore think ..." Can you read that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I therefore think that the proposal of the president that this be considered as a suggestion, not to say initiative, to weigh who is in favour and who is against. I personally think we would act not only unconstitutionally and unlawfully if we opted for this solution, but we would actually venture into a pioneering exploit, which is something beyond world practice."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the speaker, Mr. Krajisnik, is trying to finish this on a conciliatory note, saying: "We should task our ministry with this initiative, so they would contact the Main Staff, and, together with them, analyse the situation, forward it to the Constitutional Committee, which would submit this to the Assembly for deliberation." And then they voted for this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a big mistake. An operative staff cannot manage the judiciary. I think they were wrong in involving the Main Staff. The General Staff has its own departments, one of them in charge of the military judiciary, but these people were operations officers. They controlled the army. They could not control the judiciary. I think it was a big mistake that the initiative of the Ministry of Justice was not accepted in early July. There would have been much, much lower crime rates, and all of them would have been prosecuted, and we would now be able to present to this Court the result of these prosecutions and trials.
