utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. Minister, that we will be able to present this. I think the combined sentences given to Serbian perpetrators of crimes against Muslims and Croats amount to hundreds of years. Do you know of a single sentence handed down to a Muslim or a Croat who had done something against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that such judgements exist, but I'm trying to be self-critical. If we had started this earlier, there would have been fewer crimes and these judgements would have served as a deterrent to others. Now, as far as the Muslim side is concerned, I don't know of any prosecutions. I just don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did confirm that the killer of the Serbian wedding party member, Ramiz Delalic, or Ismet, was portrayed as a hero and invited to a TV show, but then Celo and the other Delalic were liquidated later?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Juka Prazina was killed in Belgium, and Caco was killed in Sarajevo. Caco, the one who ran camps near Trebevic, whereas Ramiz Delalic was also killed in an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they did not live long; not because of their crimes against the Serbs, but because they had turned against Avdo Hebib and the Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are criminal show-downs within the federation. I don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we done with this document? Is there anything the Trial Chamber wants to know with regard to this? Can we have it admitted, and move on to another one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, by the number you gave, this has already been admitted as a Prosecution exhibit. And I have some further questions. Can we go back to the portion where Mr. Mandic spoke; probably page 91 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe 92. Yes, that's right, and it's 88 in Serbian -- 89 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the latter part of your speech, I note the passage which goes like this: I'll read out: "I think that at this moment we really need ... there are terrible practical problems, conflicts of jurisdiction. Was the man who committed a crime in the morning on leave or on holiday? Is he a civilian or a military conscript?" Et cetera. Did you see that passage, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I'm following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand a bit further on this? At the time, did you have these soldiers who were commuting from home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, Your Honour, there were lulls when troops went home to wash, to take a change of clothes, or they got home leave from the army. The rule was that when a conscript leaves his position to go home, if he was on official leave, he was under the jurisdiction of the army, or if he was going home -- going back to his position from home when he committed a crime, he was still under the jurisdiction of the army. However, this was not quite clear to everyone, and the authorities in charge of prosecution, the civilian and the military police, did not always understand who had jurisdiction over individuals who perpetrated crimes. But, in fact, everyone who committed a crime in a war zone or related to war activities fell under the jurisdiction of military authorities. We complied at the time with the Criminal Code of the Federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. My next question is related to the last part of your intervention, which goes like this: I quote: "Judges came to see me, complaining of the way on-site investigations were carried out. A military police and a military investigation officer go to the site. They say, This is a civilian. He refuses to do the job, so he goes back, then others go to the site, but until they do, things get complicated. It creates great problems." Could you explain further what this means to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a report is received of an incident involving a crime, it's usually the civilian police who goes -- who go on-site to investigate; and the police officer, if he's aware of the Criminal Code and criminal law, is able to decide whether the incident falls under the jurisdiction of the military or the civilian prosecutor, the military or the civilian judiciary. In the former Yugoslavia, investigative actions were not led by the prosecutor, but by the investigating judge; and these on-site investigations were done under the jurisdiction of the Court. There were special judges for that, and it would be determined on-site who is or isn't in charge. If the one who came first is not -- does not have jurisdiction and he leaves, then before the one who is really in charge arrives, clues the superior the site is tampered with, evidence is destroyed. And I tried to prevent this sort of thing happening for the judiciary to function more efficiently. Now, another problem was that the military command took judges from the ranks of already-elected civilian judiciary, and they had the right to do that. They had the right to mobilise people. And thus, for instance, Rajko Colovic, who was a judge of the Regular Court in Vlasenica, left to become the president of the Military Court in Han Pijesak, and there was an exchange and spill-over and turn-over of staff between the two branches of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What time-frame are you talking about when you testified about Judge Colovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Summer 1992, when Mr. Colovic was elected president of the State Commission for Exchanges. He left to become the president of the Regular Court in Vlasenica. And very soon after, he left again to become the president of the Military Court in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one further -- two further questions: Who did you mean by "military investigators," separate from military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are military investigating judges. You have to understand that the on-site investigation was not conducted by a prosecutor, but by an investigating judge. That was a category of judges that existed in the former Yugoslavia. And only investigating judges dealt with on-site investigations. They would make protocols of crime-scene investigations, and they would submit it to the prosecutor, who then decided whether to start a prosecution or not. All the evidence collected by the forensics, by scene-of-crime officers, would be included in that report. And when the whole file is complete, the investigating judge submits it to the prosecutor, who decides whether elements of the crime -- elements of crime are in existence and sufficient to start a criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was the Military Court or judiciary and/or military investigating judge in existence by the time of this speech in, i.e., November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were both the military judiciary and military prosecutors' offices. They were not well-organised and they didn't work well, because the judiciary and military prisons were organised attached to prisons, and every corps had their judicial organ. The Krajina Corps had its own, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had its own. And it was not very efficient. It was not well-organised. And crimes and criminals proliferated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I draw the attention of the parties, and primarily the attention of the Trial Chamber, to pages 13 and 14 of this document, where Mr. Mandic says: "I will briefly inform you that in the past five or six Assembly sessions, out of 100 items on the agenda, 90 dealt with the judiciary and administration. And 10 of us from the Department of The judiciary and Administration worked as best as we could, and we chased the local officials to get them to establish proper judicial organs. We insisted that this should be discussed by the government. In fact, somebody insisted that this should be submitted to the government for their decision, but I opposed this because it should be done by the Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you opposed the idea that the government should be in charge of appointing judges?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that would have meant that executive authority would interfere with legislative authority and judicial authority. That would have been wrong. The government is the executive branch of power. They should not decide about judges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this document is already in evidence, can we see 1D2088. I'm not sure it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just want to show how many of you worked in the judiciary. It's a list of employees in the Ministry of Justice in December 1992. Tell us, very briefly -- we also see the head of bookkeeping, et cetera. Just tell us, by end 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's 16250, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I may, in connection with the Court's question about the time-frame regarding Mr. Colovic and his movement in connection with the Exchange Commission and judgeships, it may be in -- there's a reference to Mr. Colovic in the 9 June government session, the exhibit number which I don't have at the moment but can get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the entire staff of the Ministry of Justice in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, there were 21 people working at the Ministry of Justice. If you take into account that the last six persons were drivers, who finished only high school, and that numbers 9 to 17 were technical services, you will realise that there were only 10 people who established the judicial organs in 1992. We worked 10, 12 hours a day. We were constantly in communication with regions. We talked to future judges and prosecutors. We started out with one car and had three cars by the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's recorded as you worked 10, 12 hours. You said "16 hours a day." You worked 16 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 16 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can better understand you now, because that's what we are doing now; we are working 16 hours a day here. Can we have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is already in evidence. The session was held on the 23rd and 24th November, and the Trial Chamber will find all of it interesting. May I now ask for 65 ter 127 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: Do you remember, Minister, that you made appeals in the media for persons who had passed the bar exam to speak up? And I think that we discussed it over the past few days.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether this is the 17th Presidency Session on the 11th of July? And then I'd like to look at items 2 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: AD or items on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Items on the agenda. And then we'll deal with item 2.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Agenda: "1. Adoption of the minutes of the 15th Session. "2. Issuing a public statement to the people on the question of moving and retaining people."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It was concluded that a decision be adopted on the signing of a proclamation and the moving out and retention of citizens from certain parts of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on guarantees and safety, on condition that the people be disarmed, hostile activities cease, and peace be established."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is meant are the Muslims and Croats who live in our territory, they are asked to become civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read AD-3, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The proposal was adopted to convene the Assembly on the 22nd of July, 1992, in Pale. It is necessary to discuss at the Assembly the functioning of the authorities and the question of the organisation of the Serb autonomous districts."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just the first sentence of item 4.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All nominations for military prosecutors were verified."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page, number 6. In English, could we just scroll down. It's the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is a special commission being appointed here for crimes -- for dealing with crimes committed against Serbs in the territory of the federation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D444, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D2099.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the proclamation that is referred to in item 2 of the agenda of this Presidency session? It's the same day, the 11th of July, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to present this briefly. In the first paragraph, what is referred to is genocide in what was later turned into the federation, and, secondly, it says: "The Presidency recalls that the Geneva Convention states that civilians living in areas affected by war must be allowed to leave the area. Furthermore, emigration can only be voluntary; therefore, it cannot be either obstructed or encouraged. "All citizens of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of Croat and Muslim ethnicity shall be guaranteed all rights ensured by a state based on the rule of law." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page, and in English it's the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, do you agree that with the exception of Drvar, where there perhaps weren't very many Croats, one or two, but there weren't any Muslims, that there was not a single town or settlement in Bosnia -- in Republika Srpska that was ethnically pure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no such town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, many had left. We are going to clarify that. But I have a set of regulations here that shows that all the way up until the end of the war there was not a single settlement that was ethnically pure. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 186, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Minister: Do you remember or do you know that even on Romanija, which is well known as a mountain of outlaws, there were several villages that had surrendered their weapons, and the population -- the Muslim population remained there all the way up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Renovica, Vraca, and around Sokolac there were two or three villages. The Muslim population stayed there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Satorovici, Burati, and so on. I've forgotten all the names. Pale, yes. Yes, Pale is not in the transcript. Yes. Do you know of a single village, Serb village, in the Muslim-Croat federation that remained intact up until September 1992, that survived as such until September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that. I was not familiar with any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document of minutes of the 38th Session, held on the 11th of July, so we are dealing with July all the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 5 in Serbian, AD-10. So it's item 10 of the conclusions, actually. It says "Current Issues."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, could we have it in English, too, AD-10. I don't know what the page is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 2 and 3, could you have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please carry on, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Item 2: "The Ministry of Information is entrusted with informing, in a suitable way, the parents whose children are captured in the territory of our republic, that they will be tried according to our regulations; that full lawfulness will be secured, and their rights and freedom will be observed; that international rules will be respected, and that adequate regulations have already been passed regarding this matter." Number 3: "A working group has been established, made up of Milan Trbojevic, deputy prime minister, and representatives of the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ministry of Health, Work, Welfare and Family Matters, to prepare a set of regulations on the treatment of Muslims and other nations on the territory of the Serb Republic of BH. In accordance with this, the constitutional rights and obligations, international conventions on human rights and freedoms that oblige us have to be taken into consideration."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A broader debate should be held on the proposed document exclusively at the session of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in item 8 you inform the government yet again about that proposal to transfer the jurisdiction of military courts to regular courts? Minister, you know that Serb military conscripts had to respond to call-up. Do you agree that Muslims and Croats in Republika Srpska had a privileged status or, rather, that there was positive discrimination; namely, that they did not have to go into the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they didn't have to, and I know that, for instance, in Trebinje, there was a brigade that consisted of ethnic Muslims who fought in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Krajina and in Northern Bosnia as well. Now, one of the commanders of this Muslim unit is now a president of a municipality. Do you remember that we did not send such Muslim units to the front-line against the Muslims; rather, they were sent to the HVO front-line?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 09243, please. I'm not sure about this. The English seems to be all right, but 009243 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that there seems to be a mistake in uploading. Both versions seem to be in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This has to do with a strictly confidential document, copy number 7: "Brief review of the functioning of the MUP so far and outlines of its future activities. Summary of the meeting of senior MUP officials on the 11th of July, 1992." I am going to put it to you in Serbian, and the other participants can follow in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have English page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand that the incorrect B/C/S version is up-loaded. At the moment, we're looking for the corresponding correct original, and we'll -- okay. We're actually printing it out now. That seems to be the most expeditious way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 5 in Serbian, let's just see who is speaking there. It's Stojan Zupljanin, and he says: "The War Presidency makes decisions, and their implementation is carried out by the MUP." Then Zupljanin presented some of the proposals and problems that have to do with the activity of the Ministry of the Interior. And now the first point is: "The army and crisis staffs," or, rather, "the War Presidency asked for as many Muslims as possible to be rounded up, and such undefined camps are left to the organs of the Ministry of the Interior. Conditions are very poor in these camps." I believe that the other participants in these proceedings can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it's page 8, the army and the crisis staffs. So can I have page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, in actual fact, is this the basis of this misunderstanding; namely, what should be done with the civilian population in combat areas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure Mr. Mandic was able to follow. Do you like to see the original? It's a document of 29 pages, and it's now being printed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have understood. I mean, I have understood what -- but, you see, I don't have an answer to that. I was not aware of the situation there, so I cannot respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you know that top police officials fought for the establishment of lawfulness and legality as best they could?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in July or August 1992 we established a government commission consisting of representatives of the Ministries of Justice, Police, and Defence respectively, I think. They toured the area, that is to say, all of Republika Srpska, they went to all municipalities, and they instructed crisis staffs and the army to close down illegal camps, detention centres, and so on. On several occasions, they found civilians there who had not participated at all in any of the war operations. I remember that one commission went to Herzegovina, another one went to Central Bosnia, and yet another commission went to the Krajina. A report was drafted on that occasion, and I submitted it to the government and the Presidency on that very same day. I can speak about that, of course. I can confirm that. And I can confirm that, too, that the police of Republika Srpska was trying, in every conceivable way, to enforce legality on all levels on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you'll get the Serbian version, per kind favour of Mr. Tieger. Let us look at page 5 in Serbian. We are on the right page in English. It says that: "Only in one action in Mrkonjic Grad, there were 20 casualties, 20 policemen -- active-duty and reserve policemen got killed, so they took part in such operations. And also it says here that the ratio of active-duty and reserve servicemen abroad is 1:3.7, and here it is 1:3. There are about 8.500 active-duty and reserve members in the region at the moment, 142 of -- who are of other ethic backgrounds." And if we can go further down: "Dealing with the government of the SAO Krajina, there will be less interventions, and less influence will be exerted. Also, the functional system of communications has broken down." Do you see that on page 7?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This precisely is confirmation of what I said before; namely, that the autonomous districts, the SAOs, were actual mini state-lets in themselves. They had all the branches of power. And that was the problem that the central authorities had to grapple with, because they were actually divested of their power until the autonomous districts were dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at page 6 now, please: "The military judiciary is not functioning, the judges have not been elected," et cetera. This is all by Mr. Zupljanin, who is presenting the problems that they are encountering: "Several thousands of court cases aren't finished. There are no judges for criminal cases. They are afraid. They are being threatened. In some municipalities, the courts are not functioning. Inveterate criminals are being released from prisons, which affects the work of the interior organs as well as of the entire states." And then it goes on to say: "Measures should be taken at the same time to clarify some provisions of the law regulating this matter, to re-organise courts, to set up investigation centres, because this is also foreseen under the Law on Criminal Procedure. The three-day detention is inadequate, and we should consider the proposal for the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to compose a decree, prescribe a provision according to which detention could last up to 21 days. This was received in the Presidency, but we did not accept this detention by the police of 21 days, if you recall." Does this tell you what the magnitude was of the difficulties that these centres were faced with?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you say that this is a correct position and that great effort is made by the chief of the centre to identify problems and to see to it that they are rectified?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, the problems are enumerated that we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we cannot say that the chief of the police in Banja Luka is ignoring problems or that he is pleased that there are problems, but that he's actually saddened by them and that he's seeking for a solution; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 9 in English; page 6 in Serbian. Actually, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move on, Mr. Karadzic, there's a passage, probably on page 6 in Serbian, which goes to the effect: "Several thousands of court cases are not finished. There are no judges for court cases. They believe they are being threatened. In some settlements, courts are not functioning." Are we talking about a civilian judiciary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Zupljanin is talking about the civilian judiciary, but this is a back-log of cases from peacetime, litigations, criminal cases, et cetera, the back-log that the judiciary had to deal with. These are not cases which arose in the war. There were several thousand cases in different courts, litigations, non-contentious cases, criminal cases, investigations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on page 6 we see the speech of Andrija Bjelosevic, head of the Doboj Centre of Security Services of the Doboj region. Can we move on to page 7 of the Serbian, and in English it is still page 9. The first paragraph: "It was agreed with the army that after the liberation of these territories, the engaged policemen should return, but the army is now preventing that. These other policemen cannot go to the police stations to perform their regular duties within the organ of the interior." Do you recall that the commanders first mobilised the police and then were reluctant to let them go because they needed every soldier?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The competent corps commander decided on engaging police, and I have said repeatedly that very often the police would be engaged in combat and that it was re-subordinated to the military command in question. Sometimes the army would not return the policemen to their regular duties, but kept them under their control and command for possible further engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see English page number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Bjelosevic is proposing that financing should be solved at the central level, and he says: "He who pays, he can order. We have to resolve financial matters. We have to prevent any involvement of local politics, as a typical example." And then he goes on to say: "Persons that are captured or picked up by the army and brought in groups and without any documents documenting the reasons for their arrest are to be taken care of by the army; whereas persons taken captive, arrested by organs of the interior, remained within the control of the MUP, needless to say, against proper documentation." We see the next paragraph that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment: This is absolutely impossible to follow. Would Mr. Karadzic indicate the paragraph that he is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's impossible for the interpreters to follow what you're reading, so could you kindly indicate what passage you are reading from so that they can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7 in Serbian. Page 7 in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. We can continue after the break, or you would like to conclude this part of your examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is up to you, Your Honour. We still do not have page 7 on the screen, so perhaps after the break we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 25 minutes. We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have page 7 before us? Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do now have page 7. So in English it should be page 10. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic also says that: "We should settle the financing question. He who pays, he is the one who gives orders." And now we have the paragraph that the OTP also stressed; namely: "Persons taken captive or picked up by the army are being brought in groups and left without any accompanying documents about the reasons of their arrest." And now he's calling for regularity; namely, that these captives should be taken care of by the army, and those who have been arrested because of criminal offences should have been taken care of -- should be taken care of by the police. And then the next paragraph, he says: "Combat actions liberate new areas, and with the previously-committed crimes by the enemy ..." meaning against the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: " ... primarily looting, certain Serbs are also now committing them when these places are liberated." Do you remember and do you agree that during the war some places were taken, i.e., liberated, that would later be returned, for instance, Jajce or Odjak, and that this was military logic while the war was on and the combat operations were on? Does this refer to places that were taken for military purposes, for military reasons?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see here that, in this same paragraph, that they were also -- or, actually, that authorised persons opposed the looters, and they drew weapons at them; and the police was unable to efficiently-enough prevent such looting, because it says in this paragraph weapons would be drawn to prevent the interior organ in executing his duty preventing looting? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, which will be very brief. It begins with "Cvijetic." We can also use the English. Can we see the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this. Manning, personnel, especially in police station, problems regarding crime, the problem of involving the militia, the police, in combat operations, the isolation of Ilidza and Nedzarici because the airport was handed over to UNPROFOR, which hinders communication, et cetera. And they would not, if you remember, let us use the runway to pass. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, also in English. The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the speaker, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Krsto Savic reporting on the situation in Herzegovina. Can we have the next page in Serbian too, please. Yes, he says that he cannot talk about -- speak about old Herzegovina because there are no connections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the old Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Romanija Plateau, Foca, Herzegovina, up to the Neretva River, and a part of Montenegro which now belongs to the Montenegrin state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Cajnice, Rudo, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the Romanija Plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, the chief of that service says that he cannot speak about old Herzegovina because there are no connections, no communication with it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he says that there are no communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He goes on to say the capability of the police is in close connection with the establishment of authority, which is still not operational, while reserve police units are holding the front combat lines. He then goes on to say that 10 have been killed and 35 wounded, and that neither the civilian or the military prosecutors' offices is functioning in this territory. It is impossible to get paramilitary formations out of Trebinje, for example, so that it is imperatively necessary to demand that either they be put under the command of the Army of the Serb Republic or that they leave the territory. Do you remember that we arrested a group there precisely in his Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, here in the indictment, in the joint criminal enterprise, along with my own name, are also mentioned some persons whom we arrested; a certain Zuca and some members of paramilitary units, et cetera. Do you know of a single paramilitary unit that we tolerated the moment we knew about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in 1992, in the summer, the police arrested some Yellow Wasps in Zvornik, and Zuca was one of them. I know that the army arrested Chetniks, or people who called themselves Seselj's men, at the Jewish cemetery. And I know that very often there were conflicts -- clashes between the army troops and the paramilitary units which did not wish to put themselves under the command of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here, distinguished Mr. Tieger has shown a picture from 1992, towards the end of the war, of me meeting Arkan and his unit. Do you remember that in 1991 -- sorry, in 1995 -- that, in 1991, Arkan was arrested by the Croatian authorities, but they did not file a criminal complaint against him, but exchanged him, because there was no criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Raznatovic was arrested in Zagreb as the leader of the Delijas, the fans of the Red Star Soccer Club. And as far as I know, he was released and returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1995, was there a single criminal complaint filed against him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that his unit operated in a quite -- that it struck one, actually, as quite disciplined and quite well-equipped, the one that we saw on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the autumn of 1991, against us were arranged 3 million Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 5 million inhabitants of Croatia, and the NATO, in the autumn of 1995, just before the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the Republika Srpska was bombarded by the NATO Alliance. The Bosnian Serbs were at war with the Bosnian Muslims, of whom there were, together with the Bosnian Croats, around 3 million. That I know. Immediately before the Flash and Storm operations in Croatia, they were at war with -- Croatia was at war with the Serbs from the Krajina there and also with the Serbs across the Una River in the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the fall of so many municipalities in the Krajina, in Glamoc, Grahovo -- of Glamoc, Grahovo, Mrkonjic Grad, Sanski Most, Kljuc, et cetera, that it was a tragedy, and that it was a case of extreme necessity, and the last-ditch defence of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state an opinion on that issue. I'm not familiar with the subject-matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that that autumn, from September until the peace agreement was concluded in October, quite a few of these municipalities and large areas fell?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the regular Croatia Army arrived 16 kilometres from Banja Luka, that it cleansed all the Krajina of Serbs, and that General Ante Gotovina switched on and switched off lights some 16 kilometres from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that, at that time, Arkan was there and fought under the command of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that he or his unit committed any crimes or a single crime in the autumn of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the waging of war by Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, is concerned, I practically know nothing about it, and especially not about what he did in 1995. I have no information whatsoever to whom he was subordinated, in what way, or any other information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall see about that with somebody else. Can we now see the next page in both English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the page changes, Mr. Mandic: You confirmed that from 1991 to 1995 there was not a single complaint against Raznatovic, or Arkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked by Mr. Karadzic whether there were any criminal reports. Well, probably in Belgrade, where he lived, in Serbia, some criminal reports might have been filed, but I, myself, was not aware that he was subject to criminal proceedings at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said not to your knowledge, but my question was: As long as there's an information, you don't need a complaint from somebody else in order to start investigation or prosecution? Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we're talking about the period from 1992 to 1995, I was living and working in Belgrade at the time. As far as I know at that time in Serbia, there were no criminal proceedings against Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, in the regular prosecutors' offices and courts. As for other places, I have no information. And that's what I told Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it there. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Minister, that Mr. Raznatovic was not in Republika Srpska from the 10th of April, when he was in Zvornik, until the autumn of 1995, when he came to help in the Krajina when these municipalities fell?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of Their Honours and for your sake, Mr. President, I'll say that all I know is that in March there was an incident and a conflict in Bijeljina, when members of the Presidency, that is, Biljana Plavsic and Fikret Abdic, together with Simovic, went to Bijeljina. Then I saw that Zeljko Raznatovic was in Bijeljina with his unit. After this, I did not have an opportunity to learn anything about his movements either in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Croatia or anywhere else. You know, Mr. President, that as of December 1992, I lived in Belgrade, where I was the chief of the Office for Refugees and for the Wounded, and so I had no knowledge of these events, especially not in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that my learned friend, Mr. Tieger, played a conversation between a secretary in the MUP and Raznatovic of the 16th of April, and that she did not know who was in control of Zvornik, and he was saying that he had already left Zvornik? This was on the 16th of April, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we clarified this when Mr. Tieger insisted. This had to do with the capture of a driver who took a family to Belgrade, and there were Muslims involved, and this lady, Radmila - not Radmila Radovcic who was my secretary, but another Radmila - spoke to Raznatovic. At that time, we did not establish where he was. He didn't know what had happened in Zvornik. We were looking for that young man to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he was certainly not in Zvornik because he was trying to get through to Zvornik on the phone, without any success? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from that conversation we concluded he was not in Zvornik, because he was trying to contact Zvornik to learn what was going on there. But where he actually was was something we couldn't establish based on that intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Army of Republika Srpska was critical, not to say hostile, towards Arkan and that the Croatian Army was hostile towards Arkan; and had they had any grounds for doing so, they would have filed a criminal report against him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain that there was enmity and disagreement among all the paramilitary units and the Army of Republika Srpska. As regards the Croatian Army, I don't know, and I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that after we arrested the Yellow Wasps and reported them, the Yellow Wasps were tried in Serbia for war crimes committed in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In some of the trials here, as I've seen in the judgements or in the testimonies, the OTP suggested that we arrested them because they were stealing vehicles. However, it can be seen from the criminal report that the car keys were found in their possession only after their arrest. Was our criminal report, which we sent to Serbia, was it drawn up because of thefts of cars or because of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic issued the order that these Wasps, or whatever they were called, be arrested because of the crimes they had committed; that is, rapes, murders, looting of property, and destruction of property of the population that had fled. This is the first time I've heard of these cars or vehicles, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 13 in English, and it's the page we see in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see the name "Aleksandar Pantic" here. It's page 13 in English. He's again reporting on the situation in Bijeljina. He says it's a transit area, that paramilitary units hang around there, that members of the Red Berets launched two attacks on the police station in Brcko but were then disarmed. Do you agree that there were groups buying red berets and parading around wearing these red berets, and that this had nothing to do with the police from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These paramilitary units gave themselves different names and dressed in different ways. They wore red caps or Serbian "sajkaca" caps and other parts of Serbian national costume. As to who these Red Berets were, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, we see that this gentleman, Mr. Pantic, is complaining that although check-points are in place, criminals bypass the check-points very skillfully, and he agrees with the description of the difficulties encountered in other centres. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can skip over page 14. It's 14 in English, so let's look at page 15, where Mr. Jesuric, the chief of the Department for Foreign Nationals and Passports, reports on matters within his purview, but these are not so important as regards the hunting down of criminals. So let's move on, two pages further on in the Serbian version. Yes. Do we have page 14 in English? Mr. Stanisic, Mico Stanisic, minister -- no, the Serbian page was the one we had before. That's the right page, yes. But in English I don't see where Mico Stanisic begins. Probably page 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 14. Yes, yes, this is where it begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic is summing up what was heard at the meeting, and in the second paragraph it says: "He emphasised that the government was working on a new political-territorial division of the Serb Republic in order to avoid the previously necessary forms of Serb autonomous districts and regions and to introduce districts." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then he goes on to describe the difficult conditions in which work and life went on, and he says that Ustasha arriving from Croatia and Sandzak, strengthening the Muslim-Croat coalition. Do you remember that up to 60.000 members of the regular Croatian army were present in Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Croats crossed the Rivers Sava and Una in the border villages and that they engaged in combat, but I don't know what numbers were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you agree that these guards brigades from Split and Dubrovnik entered Bosnia-Herzegovina from the south and that there were as many as 60.000 of them at times?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they entered the territory of Herzegovina from Dubrovnik, Split, and Omarska, but I really don't know the numbers of those who did so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 13 in Serbian and 15 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this passage: "In spite of all this, we have to do our best, and we have to be responsible for our area of competency. There is constant discussion of the need to prevent looting, to maintain law and order, to ensure the security of citizens, and so on, but it must be kept in mind that certain obstacles have to be removed and that the conditions have to be created for the more efficient work of the organs of the interior," and so on. "As military courts are not functioning, a soldier arrested for committing a crime is afterwards released and he goes back to his unit," and so on and so forth. "In order to discover and prevent crimes, the check-points are still not functioning efficiently. And bearing in mind that the army's participating in the check-points --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 16 in English. Page 16 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The minister is referring to ordinary soldiers manning the check-points, not the commands; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He says: "Otherwise, the basic thing from which we will not depart is that the Ministry of the Interior is a professional organisation, that is, a professional police force, without any influence of politics, which means individuals, groups, parties." After that: "The Presidency of the Serb Republic adopted the decision, forbidding party activities in a war regime." And then he says: "The Ministry of the Interior will survive or disappear, depending on whether a state is established and continues to exist." So do you recall that at the request of Prime Minister Djeric I put on hold the work of the Serbian Democratic Party, but many other parties became active, so I reactivated the Serbian Democratic Party in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 14 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "In order to establish full constitutionality and legality, we've decided to prevent crimes committed not only by civilians, but also by soldiers and officers, active policemen, members of the Ministry of the Interior who committed crimes." Minister, can we say that this police leadership was turning a blind eye to the commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Serbian police was doing its job professionally and according to the law. One of the reasons of the conflict -- for the conflict between Mico Stanisic, the minister of the police, and Biljana Plavsic, a member of the Presidency, was that Stanisic ordered arrests and prosecutions of paramilitary units, and Biljana Plavsic opposed this. She called on those paramilitary units to come and enter the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was a big problem because she was in a position of authority at that time and had influence among the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 18 - it's 17 in English - where Drago Borovcanin is speaking. And the sentence I'm interested in is on page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He puts a question, Drago Borovcanin. Page 18 in English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Who was in charge of issuing certificates or documents for various convoys?" He asked that this issue be regulated. Then he also raised the issue of check-points which should be mixed. By "mixed," he means both police and military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at what is on the screen? Drago Borovcanin says: "What should be done, and what about the Muslims who want to move to another country or the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina held by the Muslim and Croat forces?" At one of the government sessions - probably these minutes have already been admitted into evidence or will be - there's an item on the agenda to the effect that the government still doesn't know what the criteria are for Muslims leaving or moving out. I will tell you what I know about it. Muslims asked to be allowed to move -- to change their place of residence. The municipal authorities gave their permission. It was only in two municipalities that they obstructed this in an illegal manner. However, they asked for various documents, ranging from three to fifteen various documents. What happened in the government? Was it about the criteria to permit them to move or to not permit them to move?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We actually had that admitted today, those minutes. We discussed it. That was probably the case, but I don't remember what the criteria were and what had to do with that, Mr. President. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see here that Borovcanin says that: "It is indispensable that those who are involved in crime be removed from our ranks"? Now I'm going to ask you the following: If it is undeniable that there were policemen who committed crimes and that the top echelons of the police treated them this way, do you know that the impression was created, through indictments and proceedings, not only that this police had neglected the commission of crimes in their territory, but that they even committed some crimes themselves? What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. I think it's irrelevant, whatever this witness thinks he knows or doesn't know about proceeding -- about the impression gained through indictments and proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We agree. Could you reformulate the question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, since you were assistant minister in the joint MUP for a long time and for a short period of time in Republika Srpska and you were minister of justice for almost a year, can you say that that is correct or incorrect; namely, that the police of Republika Srpska did not only treat crimes negligently, but that they even committed them in an organised way? I'm not asking you what you think. I'm asking what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the police from the joint Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Serb ethnicity transferred to the Serb MUP and they worked there, so these are professionals who were involved in that line of work for many years. It is certain, like in any police force in the world, there are individuals who are corrupt and who committed certain crimes. That can be the case in any police force in the world, in democratic countries, in different regimes, socialist and others. I'm certain that in 1992 the police did not commit any crimes in an organised fashion. They either waged war, under the command of the army, or protected law and order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 18 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negus, assistant minister for legal, administrative, and personnel affairs, suggests that our report be compiled on illegal acts committed by paramilitary formations. He also supports Andrija Bjelosevic, who pointed out that inspectors and senior personnel from the seat of the MUP go to Doboj so that the MUP would be felt to be functioning, which would reflect on discipline. At that point in time, did teams -- were teams from the ministry headquarters seconded, were they sent elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dobro Planojevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have his remarks here, so could the participants kindly read that sentence, and then could we have page 19. In Serbian, we can still keep the same page. Oh, no. No, no. No. In Serbian, we don't even have page 16. So could I have page 16 in Serbian, and in English could the participants please read this: "Dobro Planojevic ..." and then his first sentence. And then let's move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's that same person by the name of Dobro Planojevic who issued those instructions on the 8th of June, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Order; you're right. Now, in July, Mr. Planojevic is saying how it was that he issued that, and once again he says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we have 16 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Crimes should be documented, especially war crimes. All crimes should be documented, and those that cannot be documented for any reason, that is to say, on-site investigation reports, photographs, expert opinions, medical reports, et cetera, it's necessary to compile lists of war criminals which are ..." and so on, so that none of this would remain unpunished. It says here that there are some cases that some policemen are fleeing from certain units because they don't want to operate with criminals; that's to say, that there are criminals at the front-line. There is a danger of having a proper conflict. And the administration sent a dispatch stating that -- what can be done in relation to prosecution, and that all should help in the prevention of crime, especially the police. Minister, does that mean that the police is committed to the fact that there should be no concealing of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobro Planojevic explained his order at this meeting, Mr. President. Dobro Planojevic was a policeman from age 15, like Njegus and like most of these people. I am certain that these are honourable and honest policemen who carried out their work professionally, since I know most of them from our previous police work. For about 15 years, I worked with them, from policemen on the beat up to situations when we had to solve the most complicated cases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 18 in Serbian and 19 in English. Serbian, 18; English, 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move on, Mr. Mandic: When we read Planojevic's first sentence, he said: "The most serious form of endangering property and looting is most often done during so-called mop-up operations." Do you see that, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did that "mop-up operation" mean, could you tell us, by paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paramilitary and military formations, Your Honour, in combat operations aimed at taking new territories or, rather, a territory that was under the control of the other warring party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, does this have to do with mopping up the population or mopping up the remnants of paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, but my explanation is that "mopping up" meant taking territory that was under the control of the other warring party. Once territory is taken, paramilitary formations are looting property from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to see, however, what is meant by the military term "mop-up." What is being mopped up, the population or remaining groups, armed groups? Or, more precisely, is this a customary term, in military terminology, anywhere in the world?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given my interpretation. I'm not an expert. I'm a witness. I can just say what I know about for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what Simo Tusevljak says towards the end of the first paragraph. He says: "Criminal reports are filed against all; for instance, in Vlasenica -- just in Vlasenica," rather, "out of 73 criminal reports, 23 were filed against Serbs." In English, it's the next page. In English, it's the next page. "For the time being, the primary task is the documenting of war crimes and the filing of criminal reports. War crimes are documented even if they are committed by Serbs." And further down, it says: "It must be pointed out that in the Criminal Code there is no mention of the authority of the criminal [as interpreted] police that is detaining people." Also, there are certain dead-lines involved. Let's not read all of this now. Let us just look at page 24 in English and 23 in Serbian. We see here that there are certain dead-lines. Number 7, can you look at the first paragraph, number 7? It's 23 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph of number 7.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7: "The prevention and detection of other criminal offences and their perpetrators. Looting, war profiteering, serious criminal offences against life and limb, and other crimes, regardless of who the perpetrators are, are priorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 6, does it not say that prevention and documenting of war crimes, and so on and so forth, that that is a constant task, like this one referred to in paragraph 7? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2, Dobro Planojevic's position is repeated: "If objective circumstances render the taking of measures impossible due to the possibility of wider and bigger conflicts with the perpetrators," et cetera, "then evidence and documentation are to be compiled, and the MUP is to be informed on a regular basis." So it's an ongoing task, a permanent task, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to recommend all the other conclusions to all the participants. English page 28 and Serbian page 28 as well, towards the bottom, in relation to personnel affairs: "Legal and other measures should be taken to remove personnel from our ranks who had committed crimes or who had disqualified themselves in other ways as members of the MUP." It's page 29, further on. I don't want to tire you any further on this, but the participants in these proceedings can have a look at this document in its entirety, and I warmly recommend it to all of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, Minister, that the police was constantly working on improving their own efforts and reinforcing the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now have P1096. That's a document that was admitted. It's a short part of a document that concerns information about work up until a given point in time. So you have the number, P1096. You can see here that copies were submitted both to me and the prime minister, and the more extensive document was left with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The distinguished Mr. Tieger showed you, on English page 3, a particular paragraph. Actually, it's page 3 in both versions. Could I have both, please. It's this part here, where it says: "The army ..." No, I'm afraid, no, in Serbian it's the next one. It's the right page in English, though. Mr. Tieger showed this to you: "The army, crisis staffs, and war presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible, and they leave such undefined camps," et cetera, et cetera. Now, we are going to see what this document says about that, if we look at it as a whole. Taken out of context, it is represented as some kind of a plan. If this were to be part of a state plan, would the police have opposed it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is not part of a state plan; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are problems that the police is highlighting in their reports, as well as ways and means of overcoming them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 8 in Serbian and page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This may be the right time to recall that order issued by the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the effect that the civilian population should not be brought to barracks, but they should be taken care of elsewhere. And does this not show that when the civilian population was being brought in, they were actually being brought in in order to find shelter from combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, yes, that is so. That is in the Dobrinja settlement, where there were very frequent combat operations in 1992. And being an inhabited area, it had quite a few inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It states here: "The tasks that we should insist on is prevention of crime, irrespective of who the perpetrators may be." And also on page 9 in Serbian and page 6 in English, it is stated: "Prevention and documenting of war crimes, with all available means under the law, to document such activities, and the submission of copies to the police," et cetera. This document has been admitted. I just wanted us to see that this shorter part was sent to the Presidency, but, of course, it would be interpreted much more adequately if it was perceived in its entirety. Do you agree that what was submitted before is insufficient in relation to the entirety of the text?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does it mean, the word "[B/C/S spoken]," "insufficient"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It means it is inadequate; it does not portray the matter at hand in its totality.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 18286. 18286, 65 ter. I'm afraid it's not -- well, it is that, but we do not see the title page. This is a document of the OTP, but there is something wrong with the pages. Could we see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, you can see the English variant, and I will read it for you. The secretary of the government, Nedjeljko Lakic, is sending to the Ministry of Justice, and he says: "Attached, please find the operational programme of measures to prevent social disruptions in conditions of a state of war, and we ask you to submit to us specific remarks in the form of amendments," et cetera. This is not the right document, although we will be needing this one as well. It is 65 ter 18286. The English variant is okay, but not the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we are pressed for time, can we see English page 12, please. It is item 23. This is not the document in Serbian. This is a communication from the government to the Ministry of Justice. And the English variant, the English version, is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having received this proposal of measures from the government, and you probably considered it and responded to it? Here in item 23, it reads: "Operative programme of activities to secure the prerequisites for the efficient functioning of the Internal Affairs Service." And 24 is the Ministry of Justice. Actually, it is page 13 in English. Do you see this, Mr. Minister? Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall the document, but I do not see it here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English page 13, and Serbian page 8. 5991 is the ERN number. The last digits: 5991. No, this is a totally different document. This is not the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This, in Serbian, in B/C/S, is actually about the staffing scheme.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the minister then be shown -- yes, now this is the document. This is all right in Serbian, but now we do not have the English version, and the document which we had before was the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice is proposing here. You, too, made a few proposals; the Law on Regular Courts, the Law on the Public Prosecutors' Office, on the territorial organisation, the decision on the number of judges. Do you see all that on this page?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also see the next page in Serbian and page number 14 in English, so both next pages, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is item 24 continued. Then we have item 25: "Instructions to Judicial Organs." Right. That they should decide cases by summary procedure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was to be done by the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you sent amendments to, and you accepted it and then returned it to the government; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Item 26 is about an agreement on the exchange of prisoners of war with the other side, which is a governmental obligation, not an obligation of the ministry. And 27, please read item 27 for us to see what it is about. And can we have the next page in English also.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27: "Nedjo Lakic is in charge of implementing this, and it is the appointment of a state commission for the identification of crimes and genocide against the civilian population and of victims of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it refer to crimes against the Serbs only, or is it a general provision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a general provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this differ from the Documentation Centre for the Documenting of Crimes in the Federation? Does this refer to the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is about creating conditions for the identification, establishment of crimes and genocide against the civilian population, which does not automatically mean that there were such crimes or such genocide, but it means that prerequisites were being put in place to establish any such situations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the appointment of a state commission to establish whether there were any such instances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 20 in Serbian and page -- the next page in English. Page 20 in Serbian and 31 in English. It is the last page in both cases. The last pages in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an order to establish a state commission to investigate extreme cases of theft of state and private property and other abuses. It is a departmental -- inter-departmental commission made up of representatives of the Ministry of the Interior, Ministry of Justice, and the responsible department; and the agency responsible is the Secretariat for the Legislation of the Government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you say that this was part of the government's efforts on the 17th of July for promoting the legal system; namely, the security and the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
